Every Brevian operating system, a newly.why: The Brevian operating systems are made up: no family of operating systems by that name exists, and no text states this. The class above them (operating systems) is real and leaves the line ending open (Windows uses CRLF, Unix systems LF), and the new conclusion (CRLF) is the one the revised rule gives, so the record tests acquiring a new rule for an unknown group, one that could exist unrecorded among the many small operating systems.

Brevaro 2 ends lines in text files with.why: Made up, so stated nowhere: nobody writes a fact about something that does not exist. It follows only from the inserted rule and the membership given in the prompt, which is how people state things about a member of a group: through its group.

A Brevian operating system ends lines in.why: Nobody compares the line ending of a made-up operating system with Windows. What people do say is that Windows ends lines with CR LF; the comparison follows only from the inserted rule and that fact.

It follows only from the inserted rule and the membership given in the prompt, which is how people state things about a member of a group: through its group. What a script should split on is the kind of thing programmers ask about real systems, never about one that does not exist.

Microsoft Windows uses a carriage return.why: Windows' CR LF line ending is the standard contrast with the LF of Unix, stated in every account of newlines.

sources.note: The article's table of newline conventions lists Windows and MS-DOS compatibles under CR LF (0D 0A).

sources.query: Windows uses a carriage return and a line feed

The Linux kernel is written mainly in C..why: Stated in the Linux kernel article and very often elsewhere.

sources.quote: Most of the kernel code is written in C as supported by the GNU Compiler Collection (GCC), which has extensions beyond standard C.

sources.query: Linux kernel is written in C

Microsoft Windows is a Unix-like operati.why: False: Windows descends from MS-DOS and Windows NT, not from Unix, and is the usual example set against Unix-like systems; Unix compatibility on it comes only through add-on layers.

sources.quote: This created conflicts between Windows and Unix-like operating systems, whereby files composed on one operating system could not be properly formatted or interpreted by another operating system (for example a UNIX shell script written in a Windows text editor like Notepad).
Some non-Unix-like operating systems provide a Unix-like compatibility layer, with varying degrees of Unix-like functionality.
sources.note: The section's examples (Cygwin, MSYS, Interix) are layers on Microsoft Windows.
